stem: A client with von Willebrand disease has recurrent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after dental work. Which pathophysiologic explanation best accounts for this pattern?

options.A: Von Willebrand factor is low or functions abnormally, impairing platelet adhesion at sites of vascular injury and slowing normal clot formation.
options.B: Clotting factor IX is deficient, which is the defining defect of hemophilia B rather than von Willebrand disease.
options.C: Platelet production is persistently excessive, causing primary hypercoagulability rather than a bleeding tendency.
options.D: Von Willebrand factor is overproduced, making platelet adhesion too strong and causing recurrent thrombosis.

rationale: CDC explains that people with von Willebrand disease have a low level of von Willebrand factor (VWF) or VWF that does not work properly. Normally VWF attaches to platelets and helps them stick together at an injury site; impaired VWF can therefore delay or impair clot formation and cause bleeding. CDC lists nosebleeds, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding, and prolonged bleeding after injury, surgery, dental work, or childbirth as common manifestations. Therefore A is correct. B describes hemophilia B, while C and D describe the opposite of the source-supported bleeding mechanism.
educational_objective: Connect common mucocutaneous and procedure-related bleeding in von Willebrand disease with low or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor and impaired platelet adhesion.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_version_date: CDC page dated 2024-05-15; current guidance rechecked 2026-08-17
source_locator: What it is — low or dysfunctional VWF; normal VWF attaches to platelets and helps them stick together at the injury site; Signs and symptoms — nosebleeds, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding, and longer-than-normal bleeding after injury, surgery, childbirth, or dental work
source_claim_supported: Von Willebrand disease results from low or dysfunctional VWF; VWF normally supports platelet adhesion, and VWD commonly causes mucocutaneous or procedure-related bleeding such as nosebleeds, bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding, and prolonged bleeding after dental work or surgery.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.15/PDF p.19: Apply knowledge of pathophysiology to client care; Recognize and report changes in client condition; Provide care for clients with acute and chronic health conditions
correction_summary: Replaced the nonauthoritative National Hemophilia Foundation homepage citation with current CDC guidance. Rebuilt the item around the directly supported VWF-platelet-adhesion mechanism and common bleeding manifestations rather than making an overly broad absolute contrast with hemophilia, because severe VWD can also cause joint/internal bleeding. Correct option changed from D to A; difficulty reduced from hard to moderate.

audit_findings.stem: PASS after correction — uses source-listed manifestations and avoids asserting that VWD never causes deeper bleeding.
audit_findings.correct_answer: PASS — A directly describes the CDC mechanism.
audit_findings.option_A: Correct — low/dysfunctional VWF impairs platelet adhesion and slows clot formation.
audit_findings.option_B: Wrong but plausible — factor IX deficiency defines hemophilia B, not VWD.
audit_findings.option_C: Wrong — excessive platelet production would not explain the source-described VWD bleeding mechanism.
audit_findings.option_D: Wrong — reverses the VWF abnormality and clinical phenotype.
